title: Which flower makes you wet the bed? | FLOWER NAME ORIGINS

entries.note: Borrowed from French, ultimately from Latin [[from:florem]], suggesting something at its best; originally the same word as [[same-root:flour]] and from the same root as [[same-root:bloom]].
Originally the same word as [[same-root:flower]], only splitting about 200 years later; sifted meal was the 'flower', or finest part, of the grain.
Medieval phrase for cream, the best part of the milk that floats on top, using the 'finest part' sense of [[see:flower]].
Phrase for the finest of the fine in society, another use of [[see:flower]] meaning the best part of something.
Germanic word for flower used before English borrowed [[see:flower]] from French; it shares a Proto-Indo-European root with it, the F and B corresponding.
From Old English [[from:blōstm]]; a Germanic word for flower which, like [[see:bloom]], also means to be at one's best.
Dutch word for flower, a West Germanic relative of [[same-root:bloom]] and [[same-root:blossom]].
German word for flower, a West Germanic relative of [[same-root:bloom]] and [[same-root:blossom]].
Given as coming from the same Proto-Indo-European root as [[same-root:flower]] and [[same-root:bloom]].
Given as coming from the same Proto-Indo-European root as [[same-root:flower]], perhaps through the idea of a blooming spread.
Literally to mark with [[from:blood]]; from the same Proto-Indo-European root as [[same-root:flower]].
An old verb meaning to bloom, spelled like today's blow, so something 'going to blow' would flower; the hosts compare an explosion to a swift bloom.
From Latin [[from:florem]], meaning strikingly beautiful, though Jess thinks it sounds worse because it rhymes with livid and horrid.
One of the Latin-derived 'flo' words related to [[same-root:flower]].
A bursting into flower, from the same Latin source as [[same-root:flower]].
From Spanish for flowery, either for its many flowers or because the Spanish landed around [[from?:Pascua Florida]].
Spanish feast of flowery Easter, around which explorers landed, possibly giving [[gave?:Florida]] its name.
Means testicle, as discussed before, because of the bulbous tubers below the soil; a flower with many varieties that people collect obsessively.
Narrative non-fiction book about the cult of orchid collecting and hunting, recommended by Jess and adapted into a film.
Greek for flower, the source of [[gave:anthology]], [[gave:anthomania]] and perhaps [[gave?:antelope]]; not to be confused with [[unrelated:anthropos]].
Greek for human or man, not to be confused with [[unrelated:anthos]].
From [[from:anthos]], literally a gathering of flowers: a collection of poems or texts seen as a rich bouquet.
An extravagant passion for flowers, from [[from:anthos]]; someone afflicted is an [[see:anthomaniac]].
A person with [[see:anthomania]], such as an orchid thief.
Under an unsupported theory, from Greek for flower eye, from [[from?:anthos]], after the animals' strange-looking pupils.
From Greek [[from:amarantos]], unfading flower; poets love it as the plant of immortality, and many amaranths turn into [[see:tumbleweed]]s.
Means unfading, from [[from:amaranth]]; it appears in [[see:John Milton]]'s work.
A type of [[see:amaranth]] also known as the common [[see:tumbleweed]], an example of wild floral species names.
A plant such as an [[see:amaranth]] that dries into a ball, lets go and rolls around spreading its seeds; around ten plant groups can become one.
From Old English [[from:dægesēage]], day's eye, as it opens by day and closes at sunset; [[see:Geoffrey Chaucer]] explained this, and Daisy is a pet form of Margaret.
Lesser-known [[see:Geoffrey Chaucer]] poems about virtuous women, whose prologue praises the [[see:daisy]] and explains its name as the eye of the day.
Wrote [[see:The Legend of Good Women]], between the Canterbury Tales and Troilus and Criseyde, explaining the [[see:daisy]] as the eye of the day.
The French form of Margaret and a French name for the oxeye daisy, which is why [[see:daisy]] serves as a nickname for Margaret.
German name for the [[equivalent:daisy]], from a fable in which the Virgin Mary cut her finger picking flowers, giving daisies red tips.
Literally Mary's gold, after the Virgin Mary, likely because it opens by day and closes at night as if driven by God's will.
American term for a skilled gardener, the transatlantic counterpart of British [[equivalent:green fingers]]; perhaps because seeds are planted with the thumb.
British version of [[equivalent:green thumb]]; Rob has only ever heard of people described as green-fingered in England.
The hosts guess it may be related to [[same-root?:bloom]] but don't confirm it.
Older than the word flower and similar across Europe; Old English took Latin [[from:rosa]], later settling on the French form. A [[see:wanderwort]] with Persian and Turkish relatives.
A whimsical term for a word like [[see:rose]] that has distant relatives across many languages.
From Old English [[from:wyrt]], sharing a root with [[same-root:root]] and unrelated to [[unrelated:wart]]; it recurs in plant names.
The viral skin growth, which the hosts say is unrelated to [[unrelated:wort]].
Shares an etymological root with [[same-root:wort]].
Said to be the first rose of spring, from Latin [[from:primus]], though not a [[see:rose]] at all.
A mashing of French [[from:dent de lion]], lion's tooth, after its serrated leaves; English names have included [[see:pissabed]] and [[see:milk witch]].
French source of [[gave:dandelion]], after the tooth-like serrated leaves; French now prefers [[see:pissenlit]].
German name for the [[equivalent:dandelion]], meaning lion's tooth like French [[equivalent:dent de lion]].
Spanish name for the [[equivalent:dandelion]], also meaning lion's tooth.
Dutch name for the [[equivalent:dandelion]], meaning horse flower.
Danish name for the [[equivalent:dandelion]], meaning a jar of milk, after the white sap that oozes from its split stem.
A former English name for the [[see:dandelion]], after its milky sap.
A former name for the [[see:dandelion]] meaning an evil [[see:marigold]], since gowan is a word for marigold.
The fluffy seed head of the [[see:dandelion]], named for its appearance in names like [[see:priest's crown]], [[see:monk's head]] and [[see:swine snout]].
A name for the blown [[see:dandelion clock]], which looks like a priest's hat.
A name for the blown [[see:dandelion clock]], which resembles a monk's tonsure.
Another former name for the [[see:dandelion clock]].
Old English name for the [[see:dandelion]], like French [[equivalent:pissenlit]], perhaps for its diuretic properties or because it looks like pee by the road.
A variant of [[equivalent:pissabed]], an old name for the [[see:dandelion]].
Another bed-wetting name for the [[see:dandelion]], alongside [[equivalent:pissabed]].
Now the standard French word for the [[equivalent:dandelion]], replacing [[see:dent de lion]], though the hosts doubt the average French speaker hears the 'piss'.
Italian dialect name for the [[equivalent:dandelion]], supposedly because it looks as if a dog has peed by the roadside.
Name for the [[see:dandelion]] from telling the hour by the number of puffs needed to blow away its seeds; the hosts note it rarely works.
Probably from German [[from:Vergissmeinnicht]]; it names different flowers in different languages, a lover's flower that keeps the wearer from being forgotten.
German original of [[gave:forget-me-not]]; folklore says a knight picking flowers for his lover drowned in a river, crying 'forget me not'.
Always a fox glove, though nobody knows why: perhaps it grows near fox dens, or foxes wore it to sneak, or it was [[from?:folk's glove]].
The Latin genus name of the [[see:foxglove]], after the finger-like digits of its bell-shaped blooms.
Scientist who proposed that [[see:foxglove]] was originally [[see:folk's glove]], which the hosts joke was an attempt to distance himself from the flower.
Proposed original of [[gave?:foxglove]], meaning fairy glove; supported by Celtic names like the Welsh [[see:elves' glove]].
A name for the [[see:foxglove]], given because it is extremely toxic.
One Welsh name for the [[see:foxglove]], supporting the [[see:folk's glove]] theory of a little person's glove.
A former English name for the [[see:foxglove]].
A former English name for the [[see:foxglove]].
A name for the [[see:foxglove]], because of its toxicity and bell shape.
A cute former name for the [[see:foxglove]].
An even cuter former name for the [[see:foxglove]].
Ultimately from Turkish and Persian words for a [[from:turban]], which it resembles; the flower comes from Central Asia, not the Netherlands.
A mangling of Dutch [[from:de affodil]], from Dutch bulb suppliers, ultimately a riff on [[from:asphodel]]; historical spellings include affodil and daffadowndilly.
Botanical name for the [[see:daffodil]], after the youth in [[see:Ovid]]'s Metamorphoses who loved his own reflection and died, a flower growing where he died.
The word behind [[gave:daffodil]], now naming a less glamorous plant associated with the [[see:Asphodel Meadows]].
Underworld realm in the Odyssey for ordinary souls, between [[see:Elysium]] and [[see:Tartarus]]; its name might mean fragrant or flowery.
A nicer afterlife realm than the [[see:Asphodel Meadows]].
A more horrible afterlife realm than the [[see:Asphodel Meadows]].
Related to [[same-root:mimic]], as the plant supposedly mimics an animal's sensitivity by curling its leaves at a touch; also a drink Rob calls [[equivalent:Buck's Fizz]].
Rob's name for the sparkling wine and orange juice drink that menus call a [[equivalent:mimosa]].
Related to [[same-root:mimosa]].
Jess's scary little bonsai, named after [[from:Sideshow Bob]] from The Simpsons.
Jess believes it is named after the person who discovered it, one of many flowers named after people.
Not named for gardens but for the aptly named Scottish-born American naturalist [[from:Alexander Garden]].
Scottish-born American naturalist after whom the [[see:gardenia]] is named, a case of [[see:nominative determinism]].
Invoked jokingly for [[see:Alexander Garden]], namesake of the [[see:gardenia]].
Named after [[from:Pierre Magnol]].
Named after [[from:William Forsyth]].
Named after [[from:Friedrich Freese]].
Named after [[from:Caspar Wistar]].
Named after [[from:Johann Gottfried Zinn]].
Named after [[from:Michel Bégon]].
Means rainbow; Iris was the rainbow goddess and messenger of the gods, especially Hera; the eye's iris and the colourful flower are named for her.
From a Guarani word for the tobacco plant, its relative, which also gave [[same-root:petun]].
An archaic verb for treating tobacco to bring out its flavour, from the Guarani tobacco word that also gave [[same-root:petunia]].
Literally daughter of the wind, perhaps for opening in wind or fragile petals; Ovid says it bloomed from [[see:Adonis]]'s blood when [[see:Aphrodite]] sprinkled nectar.
Sprinkled nectar on her dead lover [[see:Adonis]]'s blood, from which the [[see:anemone]] bloomed.
[[see:Aphrodite]]'s dead lover, from whose blood the [[see:anemone]] bloomed.
Named after the land [[from:anemone]], perhaps for its colours or for swaying in water as if blown by wind.
Another name for the land [[see:anemone]].
From Old French without an H, spelled erbe in Middle English; Americans drop the H, a split the hosts attribute to transatlantic pro- and anti-French pettiness.
Jess teases that Rob doesn't drop the H here despite defending h-less [[see:herb]].
Another word where Rob keeps the H, cited against his defence of h-less [[see:herb]].
Said with an H in British English but often 'omage' in America, which sounds Frenchly sophisticated; Rob calls the H-ful form a double snobbery, as with [[see:herb]].
Unrelated to [[unrelated:rose]]: a folk etymology turning French rosmarine into rose and Mary, ultimately Latin [[from:ros marinus]], dew of the sea.
A disputed etymology, possibly linked to washing as in [[same-root?:lavatory]] or [[same-root?:launder]], because things were washed to smell of it.
Cited as a possible washing-related relative of [[same-root?:lavender]].
Cited as a possible washing-related relative of [[same-root?:lavender]].
A butchering of the French, ultimately Latin [[from:petroselinum]], from Greek words meaning rock celery; German [[equivalent:Petersilie]] keeps more of the Latin.
German for [[equivalent:parsley]], a much closer borrowing of Latin [[from:petroselinum]].
Contains the same Greek rock element as [[same-root:parsley]].
Contains the same Greek rock element as [[same-root:parsley]].
From Latin [[from:coriandrum]] via French, like [[same-root:cilantro]] via Spanish; possibly from Greek [[from?:koris]], bedbug, for its smell, or a borrowing.
American name for coriander leaves, the Spanish word, from the same Latin [[from:coriandrum]] as [[same-root:coriander]].
French for bedbug, meaning stinker, cited to support the bedbug theory of [[see:coriander]].
From the Greek for royalty, related to [[same-root:basilica]] and [[same-root:basilisk]].
A royal palace, from the same Greek royal root as [[same-root:basil]].
Related to [[same-root:basil]] through the Greek for royalty.
Spice mix used in Moroccan cooking, supposedly a merchant's mix of their best spices, or alternatively one prepared above the shop.
Unrelated to [[unrelated:time]]; origin unknown, perhaps Greek [[from?:thymon]], courage, or a root meaning to fumigate or smoke.
Unrelated to being wise; from Latin [[from:salvia]], to heal, for its healing properties, from the same root as [[same-root:salve]].
From the same root as [[same-root:sage]].
From an Old Norse word meaning to soothe; present in Old English, with cognates across Germanic languages, unlike the Mediterranean herb names.
Also called monkey face orchid, a [[see:Dracula]] orchid that looks like a tiny monkey face, found in Peruvian cloud forests.
Orchid genus named for red species or, more likely, fang-like petals; it includes the [[see:monkey face Dracula orchid]].
Jess's favourite, also called [[equivalent:naked man orchid]], with petals like little bodies attached by the head, distinctly male.
Another name for the [[equivalent:hanging man orchid]].
An orchid that looks like a little swaddled baby when blooming.
An orchid named because it looks like a flying duck.
An orchid with what looks like a little tiger face inside.
An orchid with what looks like a tiny carving of a Catholic Madonna inside.
Little spring flowers, not orchids, that look like tiny cats' feet.
From crushing its dried leaves into snuff to make yourself sneeze when your nose was stuffed up.
Named for flat round seed pods that look like little wheels of cheese.
A yellow and white wildflower, also called [[equivalent:yellow toadflax]], that looks like butter and eggs.
Another name for [[equivalent:butter and eggs]].
A flower name that sounds like an insult, with 'pea' as in the legume, sometimes cultivated to feed cows.
Discussed in a previous episode, where Rob revealed he had thought it was 'pain staking'.
Not cow's lip: an Old English word meaning cow slobber or cow slop, since it grows in cow pastures.
An insult-like flower name for a bean with a thread-like spiral, like a screw.
Another plant name that sounds like an insult, ending in [[see:wort]].
A hairy perennial herb whose name sounds like an insult.
Jess thinks it also sounds like an insult: a hell bore.
